# Discussion

<!-- retread copper/arctic background -->

Copper is a well-studied pollutant [@grandjeanMatthewEffectEnvironmental2011], but has not to date been identified as a priority pollutant in the Arctic [@arcticmonitoringandassessmentprogrammeAMAPAssessment20022005]. The degree to which this may change in the future is highly uncertain. A growing demand for copper is near-certain [@pietrzykTrendsGlobalCopper2018a], and @comberFutureCopperLoads2025 forecasts a 24% increase in copper emissions to the European Union's aquatic (principally marine) environment by 2050. However, a no increase in measurable marine concentrations predicted, due to the ocean's considerable capacity for dilution. Concurrent global environmental change may increase copper bioavailability (acidification, rising temperatures), but also reduce overall toxicity (rising ocean levels diluting existing concentrations, increasing rainfall driving higher organic content in aquatic ecosystems) [@helcomCopperHELCOMCore2023]. It is uncontroversial that the Arctic will face growing anthropogenic stress and environmental degradation in coming years [@thyrringHorizonScanArctic2025], but existing forecasts are unclear how much of a role copper exposure will play in these [@helcomCopperHELCOMCore2023]. 

<!-- * AEPs suitability for organsising the data -->

The Aggregate Exposure Pathway model [@tanRefiningAggregateExposure2018; @teeguardenCompletingLinkExposure2016; @tanAggregateExposurePathways2018] provided a useful scaffold both for a theoretical mapping of the key routes of copper exposure to marine biota, and using heterogeneous empirical data across multiple LoE to visualise sources, concentrations, and flows of copper in two copper-contaminated Arctic sites. Our refinement of @pengAggregateExposurePathways2022's approach to displaying WoE assessments for each KES and KTR allows for simple, intuitive visualisation of the magnitude and evidence associated with each element. 

<!-- * discussion of findings -->

<!-- sources -->

@comberSourcesCopperEuropean2023's assessment of copper sources provided an excellent source for understanding typical sources and magnitudes of copper emissions. However, Norwegian data on many sources identified as important (for example brake wear particles) was unavailable, and thus had to be included as unquantified source KES: *Anthropogenic run-off*, *natural run-off*, and *Vessel antifoulants*. Reported data from the PRTR were available at the facility level [@norwegianenvironmentagencyNorwegianPRTRNorske2025], but many facilities in the study area reported no or unexpectedly low copper emissions. WWTP copper emissions (expected to be an important source considering the area's combined sewers and primary-only treatment) were unavailable for any settlement in the county, requiring the use of population-averaged data from a larger town's plant. Emissions data were available for aquaculture facilities in the municipality (see [@fig-aquaculture-emissions], SI), but no information was available on how these values were modelled and whether they represent feed and/or antifoulant emissions. Ultimately, this makes it difficult to determine the most important sources of copper pollution for the Hammerfest system. Copper emissions from vessel antifoulants are likely an important source for Hammerfest, with its active port facilities, and @comberSourcesCopperEuropean2023 estimate that across the EU, this source represents the majority (3184 t/y) of marine/transitional copper emissions. Meanwhile, @pfeifferAssessmentCumulativeChemical2026 estimates a median load of roughly 1000 t/y of copper from shipping (primarily antifoulants but covering all shipping waste streams) across the entire North Atlantic (as well as roughly equal input from rivers). 

<!-- environmental concentrations -->

Despite copper's extensive representation in both monitoring data (in Norway, it is, by number of samples, the single most monitored pollutant) [@norwegianenvironmentagencyVannmiljo2026] and scientific literature more generally [@grandjeanMatthewEffectEnvironmental2011], acquiring sufficient data to understand the distribution and temporal patterns in contamination in these Arctic case study areas was challenging. The initial systematic literature review set out to collect data covering the entire Arctic region to support more conceptual AEPs scoped to the whole area. However, during data collection, it was realised that individual case study areas more accurately reflected the distribution patterns of copper. Given that Repparfjord is one of the most (famously) copper-contaminated sites in Norway, little data on copper in biota and exposure media existed. This was surprising, although we must note that it is possible that more data on the area were available in the grey literature. 

Our determination that Arctic copper pollution was highly site-specific was borne out by available data. Elevated copper concentrations (Poor - Very Poor EQS in sediment, and PROREF exceedance in biota) in Hammerfest were present in the vicinity of a number of point sources (Melkøya LNG plant, some aquaculture facilities) but appeared generally low across the study area. In Repparfjord, copper concentrations were extremely high in sediment (especially at the inner fjord), and average tissue concentrations were higher, but these elevated concentrations fell off quickly, and no corresponding pattern of higher sediment concentration to the south-east was seen in the Hammerfest system. The use of non-spatially specific data for river water/sediment and fjord water in Repparfjord weakened overall empiricism of the system; however, as the sediment/tailings are expected to be the main source of contamination, this does not greatly affect any conclusions. 

<!-- biota/tissue -->

Our attempts to link available data to biologically- and environmentally-relevant TSE KES were stymied by a number of data gaps. Although copper toxicity to marine organisms is well-studied, the preponderance of evidence on aquatic copper toxicity, aquatic organism copper AOPs, and copper toxicity modelling [@liaoToxicityMechanismsBioavailability2023; @brixAdverseOutcomePathways2022; @adamsBioavailabilityAssessmentMetals2020] focuses on freshwater systems and species. The most sensitive tissues (gills, sensory organs, other epithelial surfaces) identified in our conceptual AEP (@fig-copper-exposure-aep) were not well-represented in our exposure dataset, which resulted in the AEPs terminating at TSE KESs based on livers and muscles (in fish), whole soft tissues (in mussels), and other potential sites of bioaccumulation (macroalgae shoot tips, crab muscle and hepatopancreas). Furthermore, copper toxicity at these tissues is mediated by complex interactions between bioavailable fractions, sensitive tissues, other ligands competing for copper ions, and other physico-chemical parameters [@liaoToxicityMechanismsBioavailability2023; @ditoroBioticLigandModel2001]. The vast majority of data reported were from samples processed by acid digestion, this "Total" fraction not properly representing actual bioavailable copper. This degree of biological and chemical complexity could be represented on an AEP (@tanRefiningAggregateExposure2018 suggests joining multiple AEPs together where a stressor is transformed). However, so doing would require significant changes to the existing AEPs and considerable additional data; the degree to which copper's chemical and biological complexity could be represented as an AEP before it would cease to be an AEP is uncertain. 

<!-- * what does your data tell you and what does this means in terms of Cu pollution in case studies (use WOE as a guide for confidence in the data) -->

The WoE framework developed by @pengAggregateExposurePathways2022 and @oecdConsiderationsAssessingRisks2018 provided an effective and intuitive framework for assessing evidence for copper's occurrence and flows. However, because copper is ubiquitous, its presence in any given KES and indeed its movement across KTR were generally highly plausible. Likewise, quantifying the essentiality of any given KES was often not meaningful; the presence of copper at any KES is axiomatic but not necessarily dependent on any upstream KES, outside of clear-cut cases such as the Repparfjord disposal site. Because the scope of the study's literature review covered only papers that reported copper concentrations but not models or flow rates, KES and KTR are uniformly scored as a 1 out of 3 for Quantification. In some cases, a score of 1-3 was judged to provide insufficient discrimination between the weight of different lines and forms of evidence, and an updated scoring system that provides a higher degree of discrimination, and that better integrates CREED (and similar scoring systems for e.g. source data) may be more useful.

The more integrated inclusion of copper bioavailability, toxicity, and physiologically based pharmacokinetic models may provide efficient means to more fully reconstruct the conceptual copper AEP with available data. Limited models are available to describe and predict the uptake, distribution and tissue-level distribution of copper in marine organisms. The Biotic Ligand Model (BLM) family is the de facto standard for modelling acute copper toxicity, and describes this phenomena via liganding to gill epithelia (or similarly sensitive tissue), but not internal exposure [@ditoroBioticLigandModel2001]. Potentially appropriate models include @wangHomeostaticRegulationCopper2016 and @chenInterpretingCopperBioaccumulation2014, which model the pharmacokinetics of either dietary or ambient copper exposure in tropical marine (the former) and freshwater (the latter) fish. However, extrapolation to Arctic species would require extensive Arctic datasets that do not currently exist [@fahdAquaticEcotoxicologicalModels2017]. 

This indicates a need for a more mature set of modelling tools for modelling copper exposure, as although the BLM family is appropriate for acute exposure via the gill surface, it is unable to provide the degree of environmental and biological differentiation that would be most suited to an AEP. Greater availability of relevant models could allow extrapolation from more readily available water, sediment, and liver concentrations to copper concentrations at tissue-level TSE, although the difficulty of representing the highly regulated dynamics of copper uptake remain. 

A further challenge was more prosaic: depicting complex, multi-source emission patterns as a network diagram presents constraints in terms of visual complexity. AEP 1 (Hammerfest)'s 6 emissions sources already represented a degree of category lumping, but even this generated a dense network of KTR arrows between nodes, making visual interpretation more difficult. Prior AEPs have tended to consider xenobiotic substances from a small range of emissions sources [@pengAggregateExposurePathways2022; @hinesQuantitativeSourcetooutcomeCase2019; @sanganyadoAggregateExposurePathways2024; @jeongIntegratingAggregateExposure2024]. Copper, which is ubiquitous, essential, natural, [@wrightBacterialEvolutionaryPrecursors2021; @tangMolecularEvolutionCu2025; @lutsenkoMammalianCopperHomeostasis2025], and moved through the environment by a range of biotic and abiotic processes, is less amenable to the format, which is perhaps more suited to displaying scenarios where the causal chain of emission to exposure and target sites is more distinct.

<!-- * way forward for AEPs in general and Arctic AEPs in particular. -->


Ultimately, we found the AEP concept a useful way of organising exposure data. In the Arctic, where data, modelling, and source characterisation are generally less available than other regions, the AEP's ability to represent both putative KESs and KTRs, and those with a low WoE was an asset. That said, the construction of AEPs presented a number of challenges that we were not fully able to address. The use of systematic literature review, which initially seemed apposite for assessing copper pollution across the Arctic, was scoped over-broadly; this impaired our ability to provide sufficient evidence in terms of KES/KTR quantification (i.e. relevant numerical models, if they exist). Additionally, as much emissions data and information relevant to the Repparfjord may be described in grey literature, this was not initially captured by our scientific literature-scoped review. A future review of copper pollution in the Arctic should focus on a subset of the region (perhaps sites of current or planned copper mines) in order to be able to assess existing evidence sufficiently thoroughly. 

More complete emissions, occurrence and biota data may be needed before such an assessment can be conducted with more certainty, but in the interim, the AEP provides a useful means for representing knowledge and uncertainty.
